research_mode: official Home Office, ONS and GOV.UK primary methodology only; each claim has a fail-closed limitation; no parcel result, exact incident location, local risk score, candidate value or business result claimed

sources.name: Open-data table scope
verified_claims: The Home Office user guide covers police recorded crime, crime outcomes, transferred or cancelled records, knife or sharp-instrument offences, firearm offences, hate crime, rape incidents and supplementary outcome metrics.
limitations: The listed table families have different definitions and must not be merged without their specific guidance.

sources.name: ONS context requirement
verified_claims: The open-data guide recommends reading the ONS crime-statistics user guide for the scope and limitations of police recorded crime.
limitations: The Home Office tables alone are insufficient for interpreting crime levels or trends.

sources.name: Recording-policy comparability
verified_claims: Changes in recording policy and practice can materially affect police recorded crime time series and comparisons between force areas.
limitations: A difference between areas or periods must not automatically be interpreted as a difference in underlying crime risk.

sources.name: NCRS comparability break
verified_claims: The introduction of the National Crime Recording Standard in 2002 to 2003 means figures before and after that period are not directly comparable.
limitations: No continuous parcel or local trend should be constructed across this break without adjustment and evidence.

sources.name: Post-inspection recording discontinuity
verified_claims: Improvements following the 2014 national crime-recording inspection created discontinuities in several crime types, including violence, sexual offences and public order.
limitations: Recorded increases may reflect recording improvement rather than an equivalent increase in victimisation.

sources.name: Financial-year table structure
verified_claims: The main open-data release covers financial years from 2002 to 2003 onwards, with worksheets organised by financial year.
limitations: A worksheet label is a reporting period, not an incident-level timestamp.

sources.name: Single-count row structure
verified_claims: Each police recorded crime table row contains a single count described by period, offence and area columns.
limitations: A count row is aggregated data and cannot identify an individual event or address.

sources.name: Financial-quarter definitions
verified_claims: Financial quarters run April to June, July to September, October to December and January to March.
limitations: Quarter membership does not provide an exact offence date.

sources.name: Force-area location boundary
verified_claims: Force Name identifies the force area where an offence was recorded and will generally be the area where it occurred.
limitations: The guide's 'generally' wording means the force field must not be treated as exact incident geography.

sources.name: Community Safety Partnership geography
verified_claims: CSP Name identifies a Community Safety Partnership area that generally corresponds to one or combined local-authority boundaries.
limitations: A CSP aggregate must not be assigned directly to a parcel or exact address.

sources.name: Offence-code reference mapping
verified_claims: The offence reference table maps offence codes to descriptions, groups and subgroups, including old and new classification structures.
limitations: Codes and groups can change, so labels alone are insufficient for longitudinal comparison.

sources.name: Number-of-offences field
verified_claims: Number of Offences is the total police-recorded count for the specified offence code, area and financial period.
limitations: The count is not a prevalence estimate and excludes crimes not reported or recorded.

sources.name: Centrally recorded fraud rows
verified_claims: Police-force-area tables include centrally recorded fraud rows from Action Fraud and related bodies for relevant periods.
limitations: These centrally recorded rows are not ordinary territorial force counts and require separate handling.

sources.name: Geographic reference identifiers
verified_claims: The geographic reference table maps CSPs to force areas, regions and ONS codes.
limitations: Reference mappings support aggregation but do not establish exact event coordinates.

sources.name: Quarterly additivity
verified_claims: Four quarterly counts can be summed to obtain a 12-month count for the same area and offence definition.
limitations: Only like-for-like quarters with consistent coverage and classifications should be added.

sources.name: CSP and national total boundary
verified_claims: CSP-level totals do not necessarily equal national police recorded crime totals, including because British Transport Police is excluded from CSP data.
limitations: A CSP sum must not be represented as the complete national total.

sources.name: Offence 49A back-series composition
verified_claims: The historical back-series for making off without payment includes a mixture of actual force data and estimated data for earlier years.
limitations: Estimated back-series values must not be presented as directly observed local incidents.

sources.name: Burglary classification changes
verified_claims: Burglary classifications changed in April 2017 and again in April 2023, introducing different residential subcategories.
limitations: Comparisons across classification changes require harmonisation and must not assume unchanged definitions.

sources.name: Crime-rate calculation
verified_claims: The guide describes calculating area crime rates using population estimates, typically per 1,000 population for low-volume crime types.
limitations: A population rate is an area statistic and not the probability of crime at a specific parcel.

sources.name: Quarterly revisions and negative values
verified_claims: Quarterly figures are revised when crimes are transferred or cancelled, and older return methods could produce negative quarterly values while preserving annual accuracy.
limitations: A negative quarter is an accounting revision, not evidence of negative crime or data corruption by itself.
